sections.body: A strong opinion gives REASONS and EVIDENCE: 'School should have more breaks because studies show short breaks help concentration.'
Adverts use tricks: famous people, 'everyone has one!', tiny print, 'limited time only!', and pictures that look better than the real thing.
Headlines can exaggerate to get clicks: 'You WON'T BELIEVE…'

quiz.q: Which is the strongest argument for a school garden?
options: It teaches science, and research shows gardening can improve wellbeing
hints: Which one gives a reason AND evidence?
'We need a crossing because 3 accidents happened here this year' is strong. Find the one with evidence.
quiz.explain: It gives reasons and mentions evidence, which makes it the strongest argument.

quiz.q: An advert shows a famous footballer eating a snack. What's the trick?
options: Using a famous person to make you want it
hints: Does the footballer prove the snack is good?
If a pop star advertises a phone, does that mean it's the best phone?
quiz.explain: Celebrity endorsement makes products seem cool, but proves nothing about quality.

quiz.q: A headline says 'You WON'T BELIEVE what this cat did!' Why is it written like that?
options: To make you curious so you click
To prove the story is true
hints: Does the headline tell you what actually happened?
It leaves out the details on purpose.
Example: 'Limited time only!' on an advert rushes you to buy. That trick uses pressure.
quiz.explain: Headlines like this exaggerate to get clicks. They give no evidence at all.
